summary: Updates and clarifies RFC 1811, describing the registration policies for the .gov top-level domain. It is informational and was replaced by RFC 2146.

eli5.summary: A fixed-up version of the rules for who may have a .gov name, which was later replaced again.

subtitle: Registration policies for U.S. government Internet domain names.

tldr.problem: U.S. government agencies had registered domain names in the .gov top-level domain without consistent guidance, leading to multiple registrations for the same agency and confusing naming schemes that did not reflect government structure.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 1816 establishes registration policies based on FIPS 95-1, the official list of U.S. government agencies. It restricts direct .gov registrations to top-level federal agencies, their autonomous law enforcement components, and cross-agency collaborative organizations, while preventing subsidiaries and state/local entities from registering directly.
tldr.outcome: The policy reduced duplicate and conflicting .gov registrations by aligning domain names with official government structure. It was later updated by RFC 2146 with additional clarifications.

facts.label: Registrations per agency
facts.value: One primary, consolidation period 3 years for duplicates

today: RFC 1816 was superseded by RFC 2146, which provides updated guidance for .gov domain registration policies. The .gov domain remains administered by ICANN and GSA, with registration policies continuing to evolve.

sections.title: Background and Purpose
sections.content:
The .gov top-level domain was delegated to the U.S. Federal Networking Council to serve as the official domain for U.S. government entities. Before RFC 1816, government agencies registered domain names without consistent guidance, resulting in multiple registrations for the same agency (such as both STATE.GOV and US-STATE.GOV for the Department of State), inconsistent naming schemes that did not correspond to official government structures, and confusion about which domains represented the primary registration for each agency.

RFC 1816 provides the authoritative policy for .gov registrations, establishing a framework based on FIPS 95-1, the official "Codes for the Identification of Federal and Federally Assisted Organizations" published by the National Institute of Standards and Technology. This creates a single official structure for .gov registrations and eliminates the ambiguity that had accumulated over time.
sections.eli5: At first, government agencies could register any name they wanted under .gov, which caused a mess. This document says: use the official government structure to pick your name.

sections.title: Registration Eligibility
sections.content:
The policy defines five categories of organizations eligible for direct registration under .gov:

1) Top-level entities: Agencies listed in FIPS 95-1 with codes ending in 00 (such as the Department of Agriculture), plus independent agencies not listed as subordinate to any other agency. 2) Autonomous law enforcement components: Agencies with distinct law enforcement missions that are components of larger departments, such as the Federal Bureau of Investigation, Secret Service, or Coast Guard, can register separately. 3) Cross-agency collaborative organizations: Organizations established to work across multiple agencies (such as the Federal Networking Council) may register if they present the chartering document. 4) Subsidiary components: Subsidiary or non-autonomous components of top-level agencies are not eligible for separate registration—they must register as subdomains under their parent agency. 5) Other organizations: Organizations listed as Federally Aided, international organizations, and agencies subordinate to the Department of Defense (which must use .mil instead) are not eligible.
sections.eli5: The rule is: only big government departments, police agencies with their own name, and teams from multiple departments can have their own .gov name. Smaller divisions must be subdomains under their parent department.

sections.title: Name Selection and Consolidation
sections.content:
Each eligible organization may have exactly one primary registration and delegation under .gov. The domain name should be derived from the official name of the organization as listed in FIPS 95-1, such as USDA.GOV or AGRICULTURE.GOV for the Department of Agriculture.

For agencies that already had multiple registrations at the time RFC 1816 was published, a three-year consolidation period was established. Within six months, each agency had to select one permanent domain and designate the others as auxiliary domains. The auxiliary domains would cease accepting new delegations immediately. After one year, all auxiliary domains would become undelegated. By the three-year mark, all registrations in auxiliary domains would be deleted, with a transition period to move services to the permanent domain. Agencies already registered but not listed in FIPS 95-1 (such as Department of Energy labs) were grandfathered and allowed to retain their registrations, subject to the single registration rule.
sections.eli5: Each agency gets one main domain name. If an agency had multiple names, they had to pick one and drop the others over three years.

sections.title: Policy Clarifications and Examples
sections.content:
The RFC included an addendum with clarifications to address implementation questions. Existing .gov registrations for agencies, even if multiple, were grandfathered and did not require immediate re-registration, except for duplicate registrations representing the same organization at the same level (such as two registrations for the Department of Transportation). However, all duplicate registrations had to be resolved within three years.

State and local government agencies registered under .gov before this policy were allowed to remain, though they were encouraged to migrate to the .US domain instead, which was the designated domain for state and local entities. The policy clarified that DNS naming and subdomain conventions within an agency's domain space remained the sole responsibility of that agency, so individual subdomain policies were not mandated by this RFC. For example, the Centers for Disease Control (CDC), even though a component of the Department of Health and Human Services, retained its grandfathered CDC.GOV domain and could freely structure subdomains as needed.
sections.eli5: Agencies that already had .gov names could keep them, but had to clean up duplicates. State and local governments could stay or move to .US.

references.text: Codes for the Identification of Federal and Federally Assisted Organizations, FIPS Publication 95-1, U.S. Department of Commerce, National Institute of Standards and Technology, January 4, 1993.
Postel, J., "Domain Name System Structure and Delegation", RFC 1591, March 1994.
